author: @freakgib
text:
Well, I recently had the option to choose a new lease car. I currently drive a 2020 Tesla Model 3 and I also test drove the BYD Seal. Honestly, I went a bit crazy with all the buttons in the BYD — way too much going on for my taste.

But the real deal-breaker? It doesn’t have one-pedal driving like the Tesla, and that’s something I really love. So... back to Tesla for me!

The updated Model 3 is great — looks nice, drives smooth, and it’s almost €10K cheaper here in the Netherlands compared to the BYD Seal. I can’t wait to get mine at the end of this month!

That said, I have to admit the BYD’s interior was pretty nice, and the big glass roof was impressive — almost like the one in the Model Y. But the Model 3 still wins it for me with more trunk space and a frunk. I’m not even sure if the BYD Seal has a frunk, but I often need all the storage space I can get.

author: @RB01138
text: The proliferation of touchscreen infotainment and HVAC controls during the past fifteen years are the greatest failure of automotive safety after the explosion of oversized personal vehicles. Touch screens are extremely useful for simplifying menus, particularly if they are menus that are rarely used, as older cars normally required some arcane knowledge of that particular brand in order to navigate certain backend settings. Using them for basic or routine controls serves no purpose beyond saving the manufacturer a small amount of money in R&D. They CANNOT be used purely from muscle memory, you have to take your eyes off the road in order to use them. Any control that must be used during driving becomes objectively more dangerous if a touch screen is needed, as it forces you to not only look, but to look long enough to confirm you have pressed the right button and that it registered it. This is why dials are better, but hey, who gives a shit about crashes and deaths due to distracted driving, look at the pretty screen!

There was some usage of "color" as re-borrowed directly from Latin later on, but "colour" was much more common already. If we had borrowed it from Latin directly the pronunciation would be far closer to the Latin – but it isn't, and many variant phonetically-based spellings from Middle English indicate it was pronounced more along the lines of "culur" as it was in French.

And you're right that American English is somewhat more internationalised today; however, there is no standard. In Europe the Oxford variant of British English is more conventionally used, as it is in most Scientific journals. Countries with lots of historic British influence like India by far primarily British English spelling, while even Canada, who sits on America's border, uses something closer to resembling Oxford British English with some American spelling affectations. Of course, if you looked at places like Japan, Taiwan, and Korea, who have had far more influence from America, you would be far more likely to see American English.
